newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian debt remains in conflict over rates.
newsitem.headline: Australian debt remains in conflict over rates.

text.p: *Australian debt futures ended the session groping for a clear direction after a mixed bag of wages data, coupled with comments by government and Treasury officials.
*Some analysts still see scope for a policy easing.

Australian debt futures ended the session groping for a clear direction after a mixed bag of wages data, and comments by government and Treasury officials, still left the market pondering a policy easing.

"One thing's for sure, we're not going to tighten," said one short-end trader. "The market seems to have taken the wages data on board okay, and I wouldn't be surprised if bill futures go into the June board meeting with a cautiously confident bid."
There was something in today's wages data for both the policy easing and the steady-rate camps, although there is still plenty of data to come before the June 3 RBA board meeting.

A downward revision in the final first quarter average weekly ordinary time earnings report took the annual growth rate to 4.3 percent from an original 4.6 percent and back below the RBA's 4.5 percent 'line in the sand'.
While this would have fuelled talk of an easing, the data included a higher than expected 1.3 percent quarterly rise in private sector wage growth.

Michael Blythe, senior economist at Commonwealth Bank, said the chance of a policy easing was diminished when today's data was combined with Wednesday's enterprise bargaining agreements showing the public sector running at just under 5.0 percent.
"Nevertheless, sustained low inflation remains the most likely outcome over the next year or so and today's data has not brought a rise in official interest rates any closer," he added.

However, while recent comments by the RBA has left the market totally focussed on wages for a clue on the next move in rates, there is plenty of key data in the coming weeks to digest including the GDP components, retail trade and the labour force.

"The key to interest rate movements lies in you beliefs about economic growth and inflation. If economic growth remains modest and inflation is forecast to remain low then a rate cut is logical," said Hans Kunnen, chief economist at Colonial.
"The RBA will need to be convinced that 4.0 percent economic growth in 1997 is not attainable before they consider a rate cut," Kunnen added.
However, Finance Minister John Fahey said in Brisbane today that he doubted that there was room for another rate reduction given the RBA's concerns over wages and after today's outcome.

Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Ted Evans told a function in Sydney that the economy can grow considerably faster than 3.5 percent, but also said that Australia's "superior" inflation performance had yet to be fully reflected in financial markets.
Spreads to the U.S. narrowed after starting the day little changed, but slightly underperformed against Canada, which continued to benefit from the Federal Reserve's stable policy this week.
